content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the edible seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to tropical America. Today they are cultivated in many warm regions worldwide. Unroasted cashews have a mild, buttery flavor with a slightly sweet note and a crunchy‑yet‑tender texture. They are eaten raw, used in cooking, desserts, spreads, and plant‑based milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cashews grow attached to the bottom of a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple; the seed itself hangs in a hard shell.
They are rich in iron, magnesium, and copper, making them a valuable source of trace minerals.
Cashew trees belong to the Anacardiaceae family, which also includes mango and pistachio.
In traditional Indian cuisine, cashews are often dry‑roasted with spices, but raw cashews retain more nutrients.
Cashews are used to produce cashew oil, cashew butter, and vegan cheese alternatives.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Cashews contain primarily monounsaturated fatty acids, which support heart health.

items.title: Source of magnesium and copper
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while copper is essential for red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Provides plant protein and fiber
items.content: Cashews offer a moderate amount of protein and dietary fiber that help promote satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: They contain flavonoids and tocopherols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger allergic reactions, including severe anaphylaxis in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Cashews are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Raw product may contain toxins
items.content: Raw cashews are sometimes steam‑treated to remove urushiol, a compound that can be toxic in large amounts.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Whole cashews can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashews can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed into salads, oatmeal, smoothies, or baked goods, or processed into cashew butter or oil. Soaking them for a few hours improves digestibility and reduces a slight bitterness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: The egg sandwich on a croissant is a buttery, flaky croissant split open and filled with a soft scrambled egg, melted cheese, slices of ham or bacon, and fresh vegetables. The contrast between the crisp, slightly oily croissant crust and the creamy egg filling makes it a popular breakfast or light‑lunch option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Croissants originated in Austria but became iconic in France.
The eggs are often prepared "French style" – whisked with a splash of milk and gently cooked to stay fluffy.
Many café chains let you customize the sandwich with avocado, spinach, or hummus.
Croissants contain more calories than regular bread because of the butter‑rich dough, making the sandwich especially filling.
In some countries, such as Japan, the sandwich is served with soy sauce or teriyaki glaze.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Egg yolks are abundant in B12 and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Eggs contribute a modest amount of vitamin D, which helps maintain bone health.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of croissant carbohydrates and egg protein provides lasting satiety.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: High calorie and fat content
items.content: Because the croissant is butter‑based, the sandwich can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Adding ham or bacon can increase the salt content.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Eggs should be fully cooked to avoid salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich warm, cut in half. It pairs well with fresh lettuce, tomato, avocado, or a drizzle of your favorite sauce. For a lighter version, choose a whole‑grain croissant and swap bacon for turkey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. The croissant may lose crispness, so reheat briefly in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried trout is a member of the salmon family that has been pan‑ or oven‑fried until a golden crust forms. The flesh is tender, mildly sweet, and retains most of its nutrients while offering a rich, savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Trout lives in cold, fresh waters of the Northern Hemisphere, often in mountain streams.
Several species exist, including rainbow, golden, and brown trout.
Frying preserves a high proportion of omega‑3 fatty acids, which are heart‑healthy.
In Europe, trout is traditionally served with lemon and herbs such as dill and parsley.
In Japan, fried trout is used in sushi rolls and bento boxes.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids help lower triglycerides and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Easily digestible protein aids muscle building and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, essential for immunity and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Low mercury content
items.content: Compared with larger ocean fish, trout typically has lower mercury levels, making it safe for regular consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including trout.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Excessive frying can create harmful compounds such as acrylamide.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added, monitor the amount to avoid excessive sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried trout can be served hot as a main dish, sliced into salads, used in sandwiches, or tossed with pasta. It pairs well with lemon, butter sauces, herbs, and vegetable sides.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the trout to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Ham salad spread is a ready‑to‑eat product made from finely chopped cooked ham blended with mayonnaise, mustard, spices, and sometimes diced vegetables. It has a smooth, creamy texture and a distinctive ham flavor, ideal for spreading on bread, crackers, or as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The spread originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient way to use leftover cooked ham.
Recipes often include finely chopped pickles or capers for a subtle tang.
It is commonly used as a filling for salads such as Olivier or as a lighter alternative to plain mayo in layered salads.
When kept in an airtight container, the spread stays fresh in the refrigerator for up to 7 days after opening.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Ham provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Iron from ham aids oxygen transport in the bloodstream.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The spread contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty, so people with hypertension should limit their intake.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some versions contain nitrites and other preservatives, which may be undesirable in large amounts.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rare meat allergies can cause reactions to ham products.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread on bread, baguette, toast, or crackers. It can also be mixed into salads, used as a filling for wraps, sandwiches, or stuffed vegetables. For extra flavor, stir in chopped chives or dill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C in a sealed container. After opening, consume within 5–7 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Nutritional powder mix Muscle Milk is a ready‑to‑drink protein supplement containing high‑quality whey and casein proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals. It is designed to support muscle growth, post‑workout recovery and provide the body with essential nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Muscle Milk was first launched in the early 2000s as an alternative to dairy‑based protein shakes.
The blend includes both fast‑acting whey and slow‑digesting casein proteins for prolonged amino‑acid delivery.
Formulations often add L‑glutamine and creatine to accelerate recovery.
Available in a variety of flavors such as chocolate, vanilla, strawberry, and more.
Widely used by athletes and active individuals for quick protein and calorie replenishment.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: One serving provides about 20‑25 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Complete amino‑acid profile
items.content: Contains all essential amino acids, including BCAAs, crucial for muscle protein synthesis.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: Maltodextrin carbohydrates quickly replenish glycogen stores after intense exercise.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Includes B‑vitamins, vitamin D, calcium and magnesium to aid metabolism and bone health.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: Powder dissolves easily in water, milk, or plant‑based drinks, delivering a nutritious shake in seconds.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Contains whey and casein, which may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to dairy.

items.title: Added sugars in some flavors
items.content: Certain variants contain added sugar, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Lactose or artificial sweeteners can cause bloating or upset stomach in sensitive people.

items.title: Calorie excess
items.content: Regular consumption without accounting for total daily calories can lead to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix 30‑40 g of powder (about one scoop) with 250‑300 ml of water, milk, or a plant‑based beverage, shaking or blending until smooth. Recommended post‑workout or as a snack between meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry powder in a tightly sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 3‑6 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-seafo.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce, Seafood and Vegetables, Ready-to-Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta prepared with a smooth cream sauce, mixed seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid) and added vegetables (broccoli, carrot, bell pepper). The product is ready to heat in a microwave or on the stove, preserving the nutritional benefits of whole grain and the rich flavor of seafood.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain retains bran and germ, increasing fiber and B‑vitamin content.
The cream sauce is made with low‑fat dairy and olive oil, making it lighter.
Seafood provides a valuable source of omega‑3 fatty acids, supporting heart health.
Vegetables are flash‑steamed to keep maximum vitamins and minerals.
The dish is designed for quick preparation: only 3‑5 minutes in the microwave.

items.title: Fiber‑rich whole grain pasta
items.content: Supports normal digestive function and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Omega‑3 from seafood
items.content: Beneficial for cardiovascular health and helps reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Involved in energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Broccoli and bell pepper provide vitamin C and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The cream sauce uses olive oil, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: People with fish or shellfish allergies should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce contains a moderate amount of salt; those limiting sodium should monitor portion size.

items.title: Heat handling
items.content: Overheating can cause seafood to become rubbery and may reduce vitamin levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the portion in the microwave (3‑5 minutes) or in a skillet, stirring occasionally. Serve as a standalone meal or with a light salad. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 0 °C to +4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3 days. Do not freeze, as seafood may lose its texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Lemon pie is a dessert made with a tender crust, a layer of buttery cream, and a bright lemon filling. The crust is usually shortcrust or yeast‑based, while the filling combines fresh lemon juice, zest, and sugar for a perfectly balanced sweet‑tart flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lemon pie emerged in Europe in the 19th century as a variation of traditional fruit pies.
Traditional lemon curd is cooked with eggs, sugar, and butter, giving it a thicker texture than simple lemon curd.
In the United States, the “Key Lime Pie” version uses Key lime juice instead of regular lemon.
Adding lemon zest to the crust intensifies the citrus aroma.
Pies are often topped with a meringue “cloud” that adds a sweet, airy contrast.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Lemons provide a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids in lemon zest help combat free radicals and may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Lemon acidity stimulates gastric juice production, promoting better digestion.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports muscle function.

items.title: Relatively low‑calorie dessert when made with light crust
items.content: Using a light crust and moderate sugar keeps the calorie count modest compared to richer desserts.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lemons, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: High acidity
items.content: The strong acidity of lemon curd can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional recipes contain a lot of sugar, which can be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Eggs in the filling
items.content: The custard‑like filling uses eggs; improper cooking may pose a risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve lemon pie chilled, often dusted with a light sprinkling of powdered sugar or fresh berries. It can be stored in the refrigerator and enjoyed as a dessert after lunch or dinner.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pie in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days. For longer storage, wrap it tightly in plastic film and aluminum foil and freeze for up to 2 months.

summer-squash-yellow-or-green-frozen-coo.title: Summer squash, yellow or green, frozen, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (zucchini) yellow or green is a young fruit of the squash plant that is quickly frozen after harvest and then cooked with added fat. The product retains most of the vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber found in fresh squash.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family and is closely related to cucumbers and pumpkins.
Freezing occurs within hours of picking, preserving colour and texture.
Yellow varieties contain more beta‑carotene, while green ones have higher chlorophyll levels.
It is widely used in Asian cuisines for stir‑frying, stewing, and soups.
Cooking with fat enhances flavor and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamin B6 and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: High dietary fiber content promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: When prepared with modest amounts of fat, it remains a light option for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Cucurbit allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to squash family members.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Excessive added fat can make the dish calorie‑dense and less suitable for weight loss.

items.title: Nitrate levels
items.content: If grown with heavy fertilization, nitrate levels may be elevated.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté the frozen squash in a little oil, add it to stews, soups, or bake it in casseroles. It can be quickly reheated in the microwave for a nutritious side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen squash in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 1–2 days and do not refreeze.
